Tomato___Early_blight.overview: Early blight is a fungal disease caused by Alternaria solani. It primarily affects older foliage, creating dark brown circular spots with concentric target-board rings.
symptoms: Dark brown to black spots with concentric rings ('target board' pattern)
Yellowing of foliage surrounding the lesions
Lower leaves affected first, progressing upwards
Defoliation exposing fruit to sunscald
non_chemical_management: Prune and destroy infected lower leaves promptly
Apply organic straw mulch around plant base to prevent soil splash
Ensure proper plant spacing (60 x 45 cm) for canopy aeration
Use drip or furrow irrigation to keep foliage dry
prevention: Rotate crops away from solanaceous plants (potato, chilli, brinjal) for 2-3 years
Use certified disease-free seeds and vigorous seedlings
Clean and disinfect staking poles and pruning tools
treatment: Foliar spray of Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at the first appearance of symptoms
Alternatively, Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L at 10-14 day intervals
For severe infections, Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
safety_precautions: Wear protective gloves, eye protection, and mask during chemical application
Observe a mandatory Pre-Harvest Interval (PHI) of 7-10 days before harvesting fruit
Avoid spraying during windy conditions or midday peak heat
source_references: ICAR-IIHR (Indian Institute of Horticultural Research) - Tomato Disease Guide (https://iihr.res.in)

Tomato___Late_blight.overview: Late blight is a fast-spreading oomycete disease caused by Phytophthora infestans. It develops rapidly in cool, wet weather and can destroy foliage and fruits within days.
symptoms: Water-soaked, dark olive to brown irregular lesions on leaves and stems
White fungal downy growth on the underside of leaves in high humidity
Rapid wilting and collapse of leaves appearing frost-damaged
Greasy, dark brown firm rot on green and ripe tomato fruits
non_chemical_management: Immediately prune and bury heavily infected shoots outside the field
Stake tomato vines and avoid dense canopy shading
Eliminate volunteer tomato plants and potato cull piles nearby
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant tomato varieties where available
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation
Ensure rapid field drainage during heavy rains
treatment: Preventive spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3.0 g/L
Curative spray on disease onset: Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.0-2.5 g/L
Alternative systemic: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.0 g/L
safety_precautions: Follow manufacturer label recommendations strictly
Maintain a 7-day pre-harvest waiting interval
Do not contaminate natural water bodies or livestock feed
source_references: TNAU Agritech Portal - Late Blight Management (https://agritech.tnau.ac.in)

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.overview: Bacterial spot is caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria. It produces small, water-soaked dark spots on foliage and scab-like lesions on fruit, favored by warm, humid rains.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked dark spots on foliage
Lesions turn brown to black with narrow yellow halos
Shot-hole appearance as dried centers fall out
Rough, elevated scabby spots on tomato fruits
non_chemical_management: Avoid handling or working among tomato vines when leaves are wet
Remove severely diseased lower leaves and destroy them safely
Apply biocontrol Pseudomonas fluorescens @ 5 g/L as protective spray
prevention: Use certified disease-free, hot-water treated seeds (50°C for 25 minutes)
Practice 2-year crop rotation with non-solanaceous crops
Disinfect nursery trays and field equipment
treatment: Foliar spray with Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L mixed with Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L (100 ppm)
Apply 2-3 sprays at 10-15 day intervals during rainy spells
safety_precautions: Wear protective gear during handling of bactericide/copper mixtures
Observe recommended pre-harvest interval

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.overview: Caused by Septoria lycopersici, this fungal disease causes numerous small circular leaf spots with dark margins and gray centers, progressing from lower to upper canopy.
symptoms: Numerous small (2-3 mm) circular spots with dark brown margins and gray centers
Tiny black specks (pycnidia) visible inside mature spot centers
Yellowing of leaf tissue surrounding multiple spots
Severe defoliation starting from oldest lower leaves
non_chemical_management: Pinch off lower leaves showing early spots and discard
Mulch soil to prevent soil-borne spore splash onto foliage
Avoid overhead watering and water at base of stems
prevention: 2-3 year crop rotation away from tomatoes and weeds in the nightshade family
Ensure wide plant spacing for rapid canopy drying after rain
Deep autumn/summer plowing to bury crop residues
treatment: Foliar spray of Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L
Repeat application every 7-10 days under wet, warm conditions
safety_precautions: Wear protective mask and gloves; follow 7-day harvest interval

Tomato___healthy.overview: The tomato foliage appears vigorous, uniform green, and shows no significant pathological lesions, blights, or curling.
symptoms: Uniform vibrant green leaves without chlorotic yellowing or necrosis
Intact leaf margins and healthy turgor pressure
No fungal sporulation, powdery coating, or bacterial ooze
non_chemical_management: Maintain consistent soil moisture without waterlogging
Apply organic compost or well-rotted farmyard manure (FYM)
Scout foliage weekly for early signs of pests or nutritional imbalance
prevention: Continue balanced fertilization according to crop development stage
Maintain clean field borders and weed management
Support beneficial insects and natural pollinators
safety_precautions: No chemical pesticide intervention is required or recommended for healthy plants
Avoid routine chemical spraying to preserve beneficial predatory insects
source_references: ICAR Good Agricultural Practices (GAP) for Tomato (https://icar.org.in)

Potato___Early_blight.overview: Caused by Alternaria solani, early blight in potatoes results in brown, angular or circular spots with concentric rings on leaves, reducing tuber size and yield.
symptoms: Brown to black circular or angular spots with concentric target-rings
Lesions surrounded by yellow chlorotic halo
Progresses from lower leaves upward as crop matures
Dark, sunken, corky dry rot lesions on potato tubers
non_chemical_management: Maintain adequate vine nutrition, especially nitrogen and potassium
Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation in late afternoon
Destroy potato haulms and vines after harvest
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed tubers
Practice 3-year crop rotation avoiding other solanaceous crops
Harvest only when tuber skin is well-cured and firm
treatment: Spray Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0-2.5 g/L or Chlorothalonil 75% WP @ 2.0 g/L
Curative option: Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.5 ml/L
safety_precautions: Wear full PPE during preparation and application
Adhere to a 7-day harvest interval for market potatoes
source_references: ICAR-CPRI (Central Potato Research Institute) - Disease Management (https://cpri.icar.gov.in)

Potato___Late_blight.overview: Caused by Phytophthora infestans, potato late blight is a severe epidemic disease that can destroy whole fields within a week under cool, foggy, and rainy conditions.
symptoms: Water-soaked irregular pale green to dark brown patches on leaf tips and edges
White delicate downy mold on the lower leaf surface bordering spots
Purplish-brown lesions on stems and petioles causing vine collapse
Dry, granular rust-colored rot extending into the tuber flesh
non_chemical_management: Promptly destroy early infected focal spots in the field
Hill up soil around rows (high earthing up) to protect tubers from wash-down spores
Cut and destroy haulms 10-12 days before tuber harvest
prevention: Plant certified blight-resistant potato varieties (e.g. Kufri Girdhari, Kufri Himalini)
Never use seed tubers from late-blight infected fields
Ensure proper row spacing for wind ventilation
treatment: Prophylactic spray: Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 3.0 g/L
Curative spray on disease outbreak: Cymoxanil 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.0 g/L or Metalaxyl 8% + Mancozeb 64% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Alternative systemic: Dimethomorph 50% WP @ 1.0 g/L mixed with Mancozeb
safety_precautions: Strictly observe 7-10 day pre-harvest interval
Dispose of empty pesticide containers safely in accordance with agrochemical regulations
source_references: ICAR-CPRI (Central Potato Research Institute) Late Blight Advisory (https://cpri.icar.gov.in)

Potato___healthy.overview: The potato vines and foliage show healthy dark green development without water-soaked lesions, target spots, or premature wilt.
symptoms: Dark green, sturdy foliage and erect haulms
Absence of necrotic lesions, downy growth, or chlorotic yellowing
non_chemical_management: Perform proper earthing-up to prevent tuber greening
Maintain consistent moisture during tuber initiation and bulking
prevention: Continue monitoring canopy underside for any early signs of blight
Maintain balanced N-P-K nutrition (avoid excessive nitrogen)
safety_precautions: No chemical pesticide application is necessary for healthy potato plants

Apple___Apple_scab.overview: Caused by Venturia inaequalis, apple scab produces olive-green to black velvety spots on leaves and scabby lesions on fruits, common in temperate spring rains.
symptoms: Olive-green to velvety dark brown circular spots on leaves
Leaves become distorted, puckered, and drop prematurely
Brown to black corky scabs on apple fruits causing cracking
non_chemical_management: Collect and compost or burn fallen leaves in autumn to eliminate overwintering spores
Prune tree canopy annually to enhance sunlight penetration and rapid drying
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple cultivars
Monitor temperature and leaf wetness duration during bud burst and petal fall
treatment: Protective spray: Captan 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L or Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.5 g/L
Post-infection curative: Difenoconazole 25% EC @ 0.3 ml/L or Myclobutanil 10% WP @ 0.5 g/L
safety_precautions: Wear full protective gear during orchard spraying
Adhere strictly to 14-day pre-harvest interval

Corn___Common_rust.overview: Caused by Puccinia sorghi, common rust causes powdery, cinnamon-brown pustules on both upper and lower corn leaf surfaces, favored by moderate temperatures and high humidity.
symptoms: Small, powdery cinnamon-brown to reddish pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules rupture the epidermis, releasing powdery spores
Severely affected leaves turn yellow and die prematurely
non_chemical_management: Select resistant or tolerant maize hybrids
Avoid late planting dates which expose crops to peak spore loads
prevention: Destroy volunteer maize plants and crop residues after harvest
Ensure balanced soil potassium and nitrogen levels
treatment: Foliar spray with Mancozeb 75% WP @ 2.0-2.5 g/L upon early pustule detection
For severe infections on valuable seed crops: Azoxystrobin 23% SC @ 1.0 ml/L or Propiconazole 25% EC @ 1.0 ml/L
safety_precautions: Wear safety goggles and mask; adhere to 14-day pre-harvest interval

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.overview: Caused by Xanthomonas campestris pv. vesicatoria, this bacterial disease affects bell pepper and chilli foliage and fruit during warm, rainy weather.
symptoms: Water-soaked circular to irregular dark spots on leaves
Lesions turn brown with greasy centers and chlorotic yellow borders
Extensive leaf shedding and blister-like spots on pepper fruit
non_chemical_management: Avoid sprinkler irrigation and working in wet fields
Remove diseased leaves during early onset
prevention: Use certified disease-free seeds or hot water treated seeds
Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for at least 2 seasons
treatment: Spray Copper Oxychloride 50% WP @ 2.5 g/L mixed with Streptocycline @ 0.1 g/L (100 ppm) at 10-12 day intervals
safety_precautions: Wear PPE; adhere to 5-day pre-harvest waiting interval

Pepper,_bell___healthy.overview: Healthy bell pepper leaves displaying uniform green color and no bacterial or fungal lesions.
symptoms: Clean, smooth, vibrant green foliage
No spotting, curling, or chlorosis
non_chemical_management: Maintain consistent soil moisture and organic mulching
prevention: Scout foliage weekly for thrips or mites
safety_precautions: No chemical treatment required for healthy plants
